lede: An earlier pass of this archive found a Thomas Sinegar living a mile from Hannah Wakefield and called him “the best lead this archive has”, because he was one of only two Sanigers in Bristol who gave their birthplace as Berkley. Then I decided Hannah was not born in Gloucestershire, and spent three days in Somerset. She was born at Berkeley. He is worth going back to.
who: Thomas Saniger, baptised at Berkeley on 3 JULY 1808, son of JOHN SANIGER — Hannah's brother, if the Bristol man is him.

case: Thomas Saniger was baptised at Berkeley on 3 July 1808. At the 1851 census, taken on 30 March, a man born in July 1808 is FORTY-TWO. The enumerator wrote forty-two.
The birthplace is exact, and it is unusual.
He gives BERKLEY — the same idiosyncratic spelling the family tree uses for Hannah's birthplace, and the parish the 1851 census independently gives her.
St Philip and Jacob is the parish adjoining St Paul, where Hannah lived. A mile apart.
And the name Lydia runs through it.

The tree says Hannah's mother was LYDIA. In 1841 a LYDDYA SINEGAR aged seventy is living in Hannah's house at Drivers Fields. In the same census Thomas Sinegar has a daughter LYDIA aged nine. In 1866 his son James christens a daughter LYDIA. Three generations of a name that is not common, in two households a mile apart.
And he named his children after them.

Thomas and Martha had eleven children. Two sons were called JOHN, both dying as infants — his father's name. A daughter was LYDIA — his mother's name on the tree. A daughter, christened at St Philip and Jacob on 4 February 1849, was HANNAH.
against: The marriage is a record rather than a tree assertion — but **no marriage of 1828 names a father**, and Bristol Archives have now read this one and confirmed it: the entry that would put John Saniger's name beside his son's marriage does not exist and never did. What is still unseen is any document tying **this** Thomas to the one baptised at Berkeley in 1808.
Their mother's surname — JONES on the FamilySearch tree — remains unsourced.
The sibling link itself no longer rests on inference: Hannah and Thomas are both baptised at Berkeley to John Saniger, she in August 1804 and he in July 1808.
verdict:
CONFIRMED, later the same day. Hannah's own baptism has been found at Berkeley — HANNAH SANIGOR, 18 August 1804, father JNO SANIGOR — and Thomas was baptised in the same parish to the same father on 3 July 1808. **They are brother and sister on the register**, and that does not depend on the marriage at all.

**And the marriage is a record now too.** Re-checked on 21 September in England Marriages 1538-1973: **Thomas Sanigre, 1828, spouse Martha, Bristol** — one result in the whole set, asked nationally with no filters. Bristol Archives read the register itself on 22 September: **by banns**, witnesses James Hall and Thomas Davey, the name written **SANIGAR**, and **no fathers** — because entries of that date carry none. So what the marriage cannot do is join the Thomas of Oxford Road to the Thomas of Berkeley. That join is still an inference from an age, a birthplace and a mile.
spelling:
This surname has now been put to one record set in **25 spellings**. The two that mattered most were the two this archive did not know: SANIGOR, which hid Hannah's baptism, and SANIGRE, which hid her brother's marriage. Neither would have been found by searching for Saniger.

**SANIGRE then went missing from this archive's own table for eight days**, because the table was recounted from the baptism set and SANIGRE returns nought there. It is in the table now, at nought, with the reason beside it. [Own error 38](/corrections/).

**And then it turned out not to be the register's spelling.** Bristol Archives, reading the book, read **SANIGAR** — a form this table has held from the start, 56 entries. SANIGRE is what one transcriber wrote, served by two sites, which is why it looked confirmed. [Own error 43](/corrections/).

bristol.head: Bristol Archives read the register, and the question this archive had been asking cannot be answered from it
bristol.lede: An enquiry went to Bristol Archives on 13 September asking the 1828 marriage entry for the fathers' names, the abodes, ages, conditions and occupations, the witnesses, and whether it was by banns or licence. **Holly Aylward viewed the record and answered all of it**, and the most useful part of the answer is that one of those questions was never answerable.
rows: **There are none.** «Records from this time do not list fathers' names, nor abodes, ages, conditions or occupations.»
**James Hall and Thomas Davey** — and «these witnesses appear to witness multiple marriages in this church so are probably church officials.»
bristol.deadHead: Three errands rested on a line that does not exist
bristol.dead:
Errands 4, 5 and 8 all said the same thing in different words: **«the father's name on that entry would prove in one line that Hannah Saniger's brother is the Thomas Sinegar of Oxford Road»**. It would have. There is no such line.

**English marriage registers did not record fathers until 1837.** Between Hardwicke's Act and civil registration an entry gives the two names, the parish, banns or licence, the signatures and the witnesses, and nothing else. This archive spent nine days waiting on a fact that the record class has never carried, and it is worth separating that from a null: nobody failed to find anything. **The question was addressed to the wrong century.**

So the identification of Thomas Sinegar of Oxford Road with Thomas Saniger baptised at Berkeley in 1808 **stays exactly where it was** — an inference from an exact age, an unusual birthplace spelling and a mile of distance, and not a document. What would settle it is a record that names his father, and the marriage was never going to be one.
bristol.spellHead: And the spelling this archive made a story of is the index's, not the register's
bristol.spell:
Yesterday this page said SANIGRE was «the twenty-fifth form of this surname put to one index, the only one that carries this entry». **The register says SANIGAR**, which is the second commonest form in the table and has been in it from the start.

**Both index sites say SANIGRE because they are one index.** England Marriages 1538-1973 is the FamilySearch transcription, and FindMyPast serves the same transcription — so «confirmed on FindMyPast», which this page used to say, was two windows onto one reading rather than two readings.

**Neither spelling is asserted here as the register's.** Bristol's is a reading of the original and the index's is a reading of the original, and this archive has seen neither: the image is on Ancestry, which wants an account. What is documented is that **they disagree**, and that the one made from the register says SANIGAR. [Own error 43](/corrections/).
bristol.nextHead: And one new record, offered unasked
bristol.next:
«There is also a marriage certificate from 1852 for what looks like Thomas's son, James, and this record contains more information, such as Thomas's profession which is listed as **Labourer**.»

**This archive does not hold that marriage.** It has James as the eleven-year-old of 1841 and as the father of Lydia Sinegar baptised in 1866, and nothing between. A marriage of 1852 is **after** civil registration, so unlike his father's it **does** name a father — and Holly has already read Thomas's occupation off it, which matches the labourer of the 1851 census taken the year before.
bristol.bannsHead: And «by banns» is not a formality — on this archive's own identification it is why no father was written
bristol.banns:
This archive identifies the groom of 1828 with **Thomas Saniger, baptised at Berkeley on 3 July 1808**. If that is right, he was **twenty** in August 1828 — a minor, by a year and a month.

**A minor marrying by licence needed a parent's or guardian's consent, and the consent was written down.** Under Hardwicke's Act a marriage **by banns** did not: it stood unless a parent publicly dissented while the banns were being read, and a dissent that never came leaves no ink. So the single route by which an entry of 1828 could have named this man's father existed, and **the choice of banns closed it**.

That is an inference resting on an identification this archive has not proved, and it cuts both ways: if the groom was **not** the Berkeley boy, he may simply have been of age. It is set down because it is the only reading under which the missing father is a fact about **this** marriage rather than about every marriage of its century.
